stories.summary: Bend is a new programming language designed to work with AI code generation by combining fast compilation (C-speed on CPU, up to 100x faster on GPU), automatic parallelization, and mathematical proof-checking to prevent bugs. It uses a "LAWS.bend" file where developers declare invariants that AI agents must satisfy, making it impossible for AI to ship code that violates specified rules. The language aims to be a reliable way to specify intentions to AI systems in the post-AGI economy where humans may no longer write code directly.

stories.summary: C++26 fixes a long-standing issue where trivial infinite loops like `while(true);` were undefined behavior, allowing compilers to optimize them away with dangerous consequences in embedded systems. The fix defines "trivial infinite loops" narrowly as empty loops with constant true expressions, replacing them with `std::this_thread::yield()` to give them proper forward-progress semantics. This change aligns C++ with C's handling of such loops and addresses real security vulnerabilities in bare-metal code where infinite loops are used as halt-on-error patterns.

stackOverflowQuestions.title: How can I detect incorrect code changes when all existing tests pass?
stackOverflowQuestions.bodyExcerpt: I'm experimenting with AI-assisted development on an existing Java application. I gave an AI coding tool a bug report and asked it to investigate and implement a fix. The tool changed the implementation, and all of the existing tests pass. However, I'm concerned that the tests may not cover the actual behavior described in the bug report. For example, suppose the expected behavior is: User A → can access User A's records User B → can access User B's records User B → must NOT access User A's records The existing tests might only verify: User A → can access User A's records User B → can access User B's records In that situation, all tests pass even though the authorization requirement is incomplete. stackOverflowQuestions.title: How do you decompose floating-point numbers into an integer and base-2 exponent?
stackOverflowQuestions.bodyExcerpt: I am implementing a big_int class which supports construction from floating-point numbers: struct big_int { big_int(unsigned long long); big_int operator<<(int) const; big_int operator>>(int) const; big_int(std::floating_point auto x) { auto [integer, exponent] = decompose_float(x); *this = exponent >= 0 ? big_int(integer) << exponent : big_int(integer) >> exponent; } }; struct decomposition { unsigned long long integer; int exp; }; decomposition decompose_float(std::floating_point auto x) { // TODO: implement } The idea is to split the float into an integer and binary exponent, so that e.g. 2.5f becomes 5×2 -1 128.f becomes 128×2 0 0x1p100f becomes 1×2 100 , 2×2 99 , or something else big_int(2.5f) is then equivalent to big_int(5ull) >> 1 . This splitting process (similar to num_trait's Float::integer_decode ) becomes especially important for huge floating-point numbers that cannot be represented as unsigned long long . Is there any generic way to split floating-point numbers into a unsigned long long integer part and int exponent using the standard library? I know that bit_cast and a lot of manual work could do it, but this would require very specific knowledge about the layout of the type, and I want an approach that can handle floating-point numbers generically. For the sake of simplicity, let's ignore negative numbers. Note : The closest thing appears to be std::frexp , but std::frexp yields a normalized fraction in [0.5, 1) and an exponent, not an integer and exponent. Note : How to get the sign, mantissa and exponent of a floating point number doesn't answer my question because the Q&A revolves around breaking down the floating-point number using specific knowledge about its layout, and that wouldn't work well in generic code. I also don't need the exact bit pattern of the mantissa, just a decomposition in the style of frexp .
